clue.text: Intemperate learner, one with intelligence keeping in the same place

indicators.note: the learner, one and intelligence hold the same-place word inside them, as if keeping it

parts.note: nous is common sense or intelligence
ibid is the footnote abbreviation of Latin ibidem, 'in the same place'

explanation.surface: A pupil with no restraint and a bright mind stays put in one spot.
explanation.walkthrough: IBID, short for ibidem, is the scholar's footnote for 'in the same place'.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone lustful lacks restraint in sexual appetite, so intemperate is a loose synonym.

clue.text: The French ship with huge ropes

parts.note: la is the French feminine for 'the'
OS is outsize, the clothing-size abbreviation

explanation.surface: A French vessel carries enormous mooring lines.
explanation.definitionFit: Lassos are ropes with a running noose used for catching cattle, so they are a kind of rope.

clue.text: Rude word accompanying a difficult delivery

indicators.note: accompanying means going along with, so the two pieces sit side by side

parts.note: bum is a mildly rude word for the backside
per means a, as in so much per day

explanation.surface: Someone swears while helping with a hard childbirth.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a birth, but the delivery is a cricket ball; a bumper is a short-pitched ball that rears up at the batsman.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket a bumper, or bouncer, is a fast short ball that rises sharply and is hard for a batsman to play.

clue.text: Fed up with food for prisoner perhaps burning all of a sudden?

indicators.note: in a down clue 'up' sends the word fed upwards, so it reads backwards

parts.note: taken as written
lag is slang for a convict, one example of a prisoner
a ration is a fixed allowance of food

explanation.surface: Someone who has had enough of prison meals suddenly flares up.
explanation.walkthrough: A lag is British slang for a convict, an 'old lag' being a habitual one.
explanation.definitionFit: Deflagration is rapid combustion, a sudden fierce burning short of detonation.

clue.text: Invader wanting an authoritative standard

indicators.note: wanting means lacking, so the word an is missing from the invader

parts.note: the Normans invaded England in 1066
the word an is taken as written and removed

explanation.surface: An attacker lacks any recognised rule.
explanation.definitionFit: A norm is an accepted standard or rule that sets what is usual or required.

clue.text: A Greek character upset, very unwell and ineffectual

indicators.note: upset in a down clue turns the pair upside down, so they read backwards

parts.note: taken as written
nu is the Greek letter N
ailing means sick

explanation.surface: A Greek person is distressed, quite poorly and unable to help.
explanation.definitionFit: Unavailing efforts achieve nothing, so it is a synonym for futile or ineffective.

clue.text: Plant found in wet territory either side of river

indicators.note: the marsh word sits on both sides of the river letter, enclosing it

parts.note: a fen is low marshy land

explanation.surface: A plant grows in marshland flanking a river.
explanation.definitionFit: A fern is a flowerless plant with feathery fronds that reproduces by spores.

clue.text: Long account about the same classical disease

indicators.note: the long account goes around the Latin word, so it is about it

parts.note: an epic is a long narrative poem or story
idem is Latin, the classical language, for 'the same'

explanation.surface: A lengthy story tells of a sickness from antiquity.
explanation.definitionFit: An epidemic is a widespread outbreak of an infectious illness in a community.

clue.text: I stop men working — an unfair employment procedure?

indicators.note: working here means being worked over, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A boss blocks men from jobs, an unjust way of hiring.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a protest against keeping men out of work.
explanation.definitionFit: Nepotism is favouring relatives in giving jobs, an unjust hiring practice.

clue.text: House for fellow a bit deficient, but not entirely casual?

parts.note: a semi is a semi-detached house
taken as written

indicators.note: the fellow is short of a little piece, losing his last letter

parts.note: a male is a man or fellow

explanation.surface: A home for a man who is somewhat lacking, though not wholly relaxed.
explanation.walkthrough: A semi is British shorthand for a semi-detached house, sharing one wall with its neighbour.
explanation.definitionFit: Semiformal dress is smarter than casual wear but below full evening dress, partly formal.

clue.text: Principally weak little devil who quivers when facing trouble?

indicators.note: principally means chiefly, pointing to the first letter of weak

parts.note: taken as written
an imp is a small demon

explanation.surface: A feeble little rascal trembles in the face of danger.
explanation.definitionFit: A wimp is a timid, cowardly person who shrinks from confrontation.

clue.text: Smart dame may be suggested by city's old name

definitions.text: Smart dame may be suggested by
definitions.meaning: the phrase smart dame is a new arrangement of the Dutch capital's letters, so the answer read as an instruction suggests it
the former name of a great American city, colonised by the Dutch

explanation.surface: An elegant woman is hinted at by a town's former title.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer as 'new Amsterdam': rearrange AMSTERDAM and you get SMART DAME. It was New York's name under Dutch rule.
explanation.definitionFit: Dutch colonists called their settlement on Manhattan by this title before the English renamed it New York in 1664.

clue.text: Like operation of mower in meadow?

definitions.meaning: looks like a description of lawnmower engineering, but is the solo worker of the song
recalls the children's counting song about going to mow a meadow

explanation.surface: A question about how a grass-cutting machine works in a field.
explanation.walkthrough: The counting song begins 'One man went to mow, went to mow a meadow', so the mowing is done single-handed.
explanation.definitionFit: A one-man operation is run by a single person, as the song's lone mower is.

clue.text: Maybe Sussex chaps in club rooms below?

indicators.note: the south-eastern men sit in the club, enclosed by it

parts.note: a bat is a club used in sport
Sussex is one county of the South East, SE
men are chaps

explanation.surface: Perhaps fellows from Sussex meet in a club's lower floor.
explanation.walkthrough: Sussex is a county in south-east England, so it is an example of SE.
explanation.definitionFit: A basement is the storey of a building below ground level.

clue.text: Better to go with the flow?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: as a verb, to improve something by making it more efficient
second meaning: to shape something so it passes smoothly through air or water

explanation.walkthrough: 'Go with the flow' sounds like relaxed advice, but it describes a shape designed for moving through a current.
explanation.definitionFit: To streamline is both to improve efficiency and to give a body a smooth, drag-reducing shape.

clue.text: What's prior to put in religious houses? Plants

indicators.note: the word for 'prior to' is placed inside the religious houses

parts.note: friaries are houses of friars
till means until, up to the time of

explanation.surface: A query about what a monastery head should place in monasteries.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Prior' looks like a monk, but it means 'before'.
explanation.definitionFit: Fritillaries are bulbous plants of the lily family with chequered, bell-shaped flowers.

clue.text: Hurry to give silly advice regarding banana skin?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: an informal order to go faster, from pressing the accelerator
second meaning: read literally, telling someone to tread on the skin, which would make them slip

explanation.walkthrough: The phrase literally means 'tread on it', which is the worst thing to do with a banana skin.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom tells a driver to press the accelerator, hence to make haste.

clue.text: Bottom in lesson with zero rating — exceptionally this?

definitions.text: Bottom in lesson with zero rating — exceptionally this?

indicators.note: exceptionally here means out of the usual order, so the letters are rearranged
the bottom of a word is its last letter

parts.note: taken as written
zero looks like the letter O
taken as written

explanation.surface: A pupil who comes last in class and scores nothing must be remarkably uninformed.
explanation.walkthrough: As a whole the clue describes the pupil: bottom of the class with a zero score.
explanation.definitionFit: A student at the foot of the class who scores nothing is plainly lacking knowledge.

clue.text: What any sweetheart wants to obtain her Bill

parts.note: taken as written
get means obtain
taken as written
ness and bill both mean a headland, as in Portland Bill

explanation.surface: A lover longs to win her man called Bill.
explanation.walkthrough: Bill looks like a boyfriend's name; it is a headland, like ness (Portland Bill is a promontory in Dorset).
explanation.definitionFit: Lovers desire closeness and unity, the state of being together.

clue.text: Hair needs two securing devices

parts.note: a bar is the first of the two things that secure, as across a door
a net is the second securing device, catching and holding

explanation.surface: Hair needs a pair of clips to hold it in place.
explanation.walkthrough: BARNET is Cockney rhyming slang: barnet fair, hair.
explanation.definitionFit: Barnet is British slang for a person's hair, from the rhyme Barnet Fair.

clue.text: Pure speed — beyond maximum speed!

indicators.note: the speed word comes after the maximum speed, going beyond it

parts.note: c is the speed of light, the fastest possible
haste is speed

explanation.surface: Sheer velocity exceeds the limit.
explanation.walkthrough: In physics c is the speed of light, the universe's speed limit.
explanation.definitionFit: Chaste means pure in the sense of morally clean, abstaining from sex.

clue.text: Graduate's publicity agent supplies document

parts.note: a PRO is a public relations officer
the possessive reads as 'for MA', the agent working for a Master of Arts

explanation.surface: A graduate's press officer provides the paperwork.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer reads in order as a press officer for a Master of Arts.
explanation.definitionFit: A pro forma is a standard form or provisional invoice, a document prepared in advance.

clue.text: Hospital cuts returning — one brings message from above?

indicators.note: returning means going back, so the letters are read in reverse

parts.note: pares means trims or cuts

explanation.surface: Health service reductions come back, announced from on high.
explanation.definitionFit: A seraph is an angel, and angels in scripture carry messages from heaven.

clue.text: Attention-seeker in job wanting prizes ultimately for nothing

indicators.note: one letter stands for the other, swapped in as a replacement

parts.note: a post is a job
nothing is zero, looking like O

indicators.note: ultimately means at the end, so the last letter of prizes

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone after notice at work gets rewards for doing nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: Psst is the hissing sound made to catch someone's notice discreetly.

clue.text: "Within earshot" may cover it

indicators.note: the quoted phrase holds the answer inside its letters, covering it

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A quoted phrase might cover a meaning.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer straddles the two quoted words, and 'within earshot' also means close by.
explanation.definitionFit: Something within earshot is close enough to hear, so it is close by.

clue.text: Protesters criticise teams across part of Oz

parts.note: diss is slang for disrespect or criticise

indicators.note: the teams stretch across the region, enclosing it

parts.note: sides are teams
the Northern Territory, NT, is a part of Australia

explanation.surface: Demonstrators slate sports teams across a region of Australia.
explanation.definitionFit: Dissidents oppose official policy, so they are protesters against the state.

clue.text: Rubbish deposited by a vale

parts.note: tat is shoddy goods or junk
taken as written

explanation.surface: Waste is dumped beside a valley.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vale' looks like a valley; it is Latin for farewell.
explanation.definitionFit: Ta-ta is a casual British goodbye, matching the Latin farewell vale.

clue.text: Schedule in heart unit

indicators.note: the schedule word goes in the heart, enclosed by it

parts.note: the centre is the heart of something
to time something is to schedule it

explanation.surface: A timetable sits in a cardiac ward.
explanation.definitionFit: A centimetre is a metric unit of length, one hundredth of a metre.
